1969 Dodge Coronet Charger SuperbeeRd Is a Shocker That'll Make You Weep, or Throw Cash at It
24 photos
Photo: Facebook Marketplace/Timofey Kosharnyy
1969 Dodge Charger Daytona, 1970 Plymouth Road Runner Superbird. End of Mopar aero warriors story. The two monikers have a special place within the sacred realms of Detroit. Say what you will, but there’s nothing like those two. Unless, of course, we take this red “WTF” (What the Fantasy) into consideration. Which is all of the above, combined into one. One of None.
Chrysler Corporation didn’t just add a new chapter to automotive history books in 1969-1970, when its two racing divisions, Dodge and Plymouth, released the mythical winged warriors. No, good ol’ Ma Mopar kicked the doors of imagination wide open, and let loose all the demons that inhabited the most secluded corners of fantasy, giving them a license to roam free wherever they wished. As it turned out, the little satans decided to play the NASCAR theme for Halloween.
The Dodge Charger and the Plymouth Road Runner were already megahits in the late sixties, so it was only natural that ChryCo would use those platforms to homologate the aerodynamic nose and wing for the high banks of the National Association for Stock Car Auto Racing. Built strictly to meet homologation numbers, the two models were acquired tastes at first, and are now holy grails worth a lot of cash. Think millions, in certain cases. American dollars’ worth of millions.
Then again, reality is that a universally acknowledged truth is the one that says gearheads who simply cannot afford a genuine winged Mopar (which is frankly most of them) will sometimes settle for the next best thing. No, I’m not talking about the base, generic, commonplace model (Charger or Road Runner). I’m talking about replicas.
Photo: Facebook Marketplace/Timofey Kosharnyy Building or buying a tribute car is a perfectly fine compromise. There are plenty of beautifully executed homages out there roaring up and down the streets. These faithful recreations often bring immense honor and well-deserved pride to their dedicated automotive passionate builders. And then, there’s this… (insert noun, adjective, or whatever part of speech you deem fitting).
The particular vehicle we are examining today is so wildly off the charts that describing it won’t suffice a mere complete rewriting of the automotive rule books. No, you might need a chaotic collision of multiple cinematic universes to even begin making sense of it. Ladies and gentlemen, behold the magnificent absurdity of the 1969 Dodge Charger Coronet SuperbeeRd. The WHAT, you ask? Yes, you read that absolute nonsense perfectly correctly.
It perfectly mirrors my almost exact thought when I first stumbled upon this listing. I will freely admit there may or may not have been several loud religious blasphemes uttered when I read the descriptions. I am a heathen and a pagan and an infidel, and also fairly certain I invoked the guy down under - and his entire army of horned and hooved havoc raisers - trying to comprehend the sheer audacity of this bizarre rolling identity crisis machine.
Photo: Facebook Marketplace/Timofey Kosharnyy I now, it’s 2026, and self-identification doesn’t live constrained in the cufflinks of that “0” and “1” duality, so this brow-raising jaw-dropper has a place here. But the mind absolutely boggles at the thought process behind this build. Why would anyone decide to build a Plymouth Superbird out of a Dodge?
More confusingly, why build it out of a 1969 car, and specifically out of a Coronet? If they started out with a Dodge chassis anyway, why on earth would they not simply create a 1969 Dodge Charger Daytona tribute to keep things somewhat historically accurate?
Instead of logic, we get this magnificent red monstrosity. We are looking at a 1969 Dodge Coronet proudly wearing a 1970 Plymouth Superbird body kit. This automotive Frankenstein is currently roaming the deepest, darkest corners of the internet, desperately screaming for attention. The seller has generously plastered it across multiple platforms, ensuring maximum visibility for a build that leaves purists weeping quietly into their greasy shop rags.
Photo: Facebook Marketplace/Timofey Kosharnyy Consistency is clearly not a priority for whoever unleashed this creation upon the world. The vehicle has been listed in three different places, namely Craigslist, Facebook Marketplace, and ClassicCars.com. Remarkably, it goes by a completely different name depending on which digital billboard you happen to be viewing. It is almost as if the car is currently in the witness protection program and needs a steady supply of fresh fake aliases.
Over on Facebook Marketplace, it nonchalantly poses as a 1969 Dodge Charger. Meanwhile, the listing on ClassicCars.com finally admits the truth, calling it a 1969 Dodge Coronet. However, the Craigslist advertisement gets the most brilliantly chaotic moniker of them all. There, it is proudly heralded as the 1969 Dodge Coronet SuperBeeRd. This linguistic masterpiece perfectly captures the utter confusion radiating from every single inch of its modified bodywork today.
The pricing strategy is equally baffling and seems entirely dependent on your chosen shopping venue. If you fancy buying this unique machine through ClassicCars.com, you must be prepared to part with $75,000. Conversely, if you prefer braving the wild and unpredictable frontiers of Facebook Marketplace or Craigslist, the asking price suddenly drops to a somewhat more reasonable $69,000.
Photo: Facebook Marketplace/Timofey Kosharnyy Cryptocurrency is also enthusiastically accepted for this completely bizarre financial endeavor, but I’m willing to bet an entire pint of gasoline that the owner might be open to doubloons, tetradrachms, sesterces, denars, or shillings – as long as they’re pure mint silver or gold, it’s fair game.
Then there is the absolutely fascinating mystery of the odometer readings. According to the laconic Craigslist description, this custom project has covered a mere 150 miles since its unholy resurrection. That is certainly not too shabby for a supposedly fresh build sporting a clean title and current registration extending through April 2027. One might assume the car basically just rolled straight out of the garage and onto the pavement outside.
However, the ClassicCars.com listing confidently claims the vehicle has only traveled 90 miles. To make matters even more convoluted, the Facebook Marketplace post proudly states it has been driven 1,000 miles. Perhaps the car sneaks out and drives itself while the owner sleeps. Alternatively, keeping track of actual distance is just another boring rule this one-of-none NASCAR tribute has boldly and proudly chosen to ignore.
Photo: Facebook Marketplace/Timofey Kosharnyy The descriptions themselves are hilariously laconic for such an enormous build. We are bluntly informed it features a 440 engine paired with a 727 automatic column shift transmission. The interior is reportedly brand new, featuring a custom cluster and dash. Buyers can also expect power steering, power front disc brakes, and absolutely no roll cage or racing seats. In case the internet isn’t a good enough source to trust, interested prospect would find it in Simi Valley, California.
It is simply a comfortable street cruiser wearing a massive rear wing, rocking Winger Warrior swagger like history comes with unilaterally revokable terms and conditions. Ultimately, this confusing machine is described as a true one-of-a-kind project and a guaranteed head turner. I’m fairly certain that whoever put this together deserves an award – if not for determination, then for originality.
It will undoubtedly turn heads everywhere it goes, mostly because confused onlookers will be desperately trying to identify it. This rolling “hold my beer” paradox proves that with enough fiberglass, red paint, and wild imagination, anything is completely possible. Whether it should be possible is an entirely different debate. One that doesn’t come cheap at all.
